lesson.title: Radians per Second: Why Frequency Wears a Different Hat in Equations
lesson.summary: Angular frequency rescales ordinary frequency into radians per second so it plugs directly into the sine and cosine functions that describe AC waveforms.
lesson.body:
Ordinary frequency, f, tells you how many cycles happen per second, but the mathematical functions used to describe sinusoids, sine and cosine, do not take cycles as their input. They take angles, expressed in radians. A full cycle of a sine wave corresponds to sweeping through 2 pi radians, so to convert a frequency in hertz into a rate that plays nicely inside sin() and cos(), you multiply by 2 pi. That converted quantity is called angular frequency, written omega, and it is defined as omega = 2 pi f, with units of radians per second (rad/s).

This is why nearly every AC circuit equation is written as v(t) = Vm sin(omega t), not v(t) = Vm sin(2 pi f t), even though the two are mathematically identical. Writing omega instead of 2 pi f keeps the equations shorter and makes it visually obvious which quantities are frequencies dressed up in angle units, ready to be added to phase angles inside the sine function. Angular frequency also shows up directly in the impedance formulas for capacitors and inductors, where reactance depends on omega L or 1/(omega C), because those components respond to the actual rate of change of the signal, not to an arbitrary count of cycles per second.

Worked example: North American electrical power is generated at f = 60 Hz. Converting to angular frequency: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi (60) = 376.99 rad/s, which power engineers commonly round to 377 rad/s, a number that appears repeatedly in power systems reactance calculations for 60 Hz equipment. Checking the arithmetic: 2 times 3.14159 times 60 equals 376.99, confirming the rounded figure. For a European 50 Hz system, the same calculation gives omega = 2 pi (50) = 314.16 rad/s, a noticeably different number even though the two mains frequencies only differ by 10 Hz, since the 2 pi multiplier magnifies the gap.

It helps to keep straight that omega is not a new physical phenomenon, it is frequency measured on an angular scale rather than a cyclical one, in the same way that a rotating fan blade can be described either in revolutions per second or in radians per second. Both describe the same physical rotation rate, just scaled by the constant 2 pi. Because a full circle is 2 pi radians, one revolution per second is identical to an angular speed of 2 pi rad/s, exactly the same relationship as f and omega in an electrical waveform.

A frequent stumbling block is plugging f directly into a sine function meant for omega t, or forgetting the 2 pi conversion when computing reactance. Since capacitive reactance is Xc = 1/(omega C) and inductive reactance is XL = omega L, using f in place of omega in either formula introduces a 2 pi error, throwing the answer off by roughly a factor of 6.28. Always check whether a formula calls for f or omega before substituting numbers, and remember the fixed conversion omega = 2 pi f links them exactly.
